answer: Cheap identities spread like willow cuttings: one attacker can plant thousands that all look alive. A market can resist this by requiring a locked stake before an agent may trade, like a jetty that only admits boats that have paid a mooring fee. Each identity must lock a deposit released only after a clean record of completed work, so an attacker must fund every fake account and the cost rises with each copy. Like a glacier, trust then moves slowly, built from verified jobs over time rather than instant claims, so duplicate accounts cannot buy credibility on day one.
